body.html: Angina is chest pain from a heart muscle that is short of oxygen but not yet dying. Three types: stable (exertional, fixed plaque), unstable (clot on plaque, an emergency) and Prinzmetal (spasm).

Squeezing chest pain or heaviness to the neck, jaw, arms, shoulders or back, with dyspnoea and sweating. Elderly: epigastric pain after meals. Women: burning or tenderness. Angina is transient ischaemia without infarction.

StableUnstablePrinzmetal
CausePlaque over 70 percentClot on plaqueCoronary spasm
WhenExertion or stressAlso at rest, persistentAny time, often night
ReliefRestDoes not settleNitrates, CCBs
IschaemiaSubendocardialSubendocardialTransmural
ECGST depressionST depressionST elevation

Stable angina also arises in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic stenosis and hypertension. Unstable angina is an emergency. Prinzmetal is triggered by stress, smoking and cocaine and diagnosed by ergonovine or acetylcholine provocation.
ECG in attacks, stress test, angiography. Lifestyle changes; sublingual nitroglycerin, long-acting nitrates, aspirin, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers; angioplasty or bypass.
An arrhythmia is an irregular rhythm. The one to know is atrial fibrillation: the commonest significant arrhythmia, and a major cause of stroke.

SA node, atria, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres, ventricles.

WaveMeaning
PAtrial depolarisation (right atrium first)
QRSVentricular depolarisation, 0.08 to 0.12 s
TVentricular repolarisation

Almost 59 million people in 2019. The sinus node is inhibited; chaotic re-entrant wavelets drive the atria. Causes: hypertension, coronary disease, mitral valve disease, heart failure, cardiomyopathy. Symptoms: palpitations, flutters, chest pain, dyspnoea, fatigue, dizziness, confusion, or none.

Clots form in the left atrial appendage and embolise: stroke risk about five-fold. Management: stroke prevention, rhythm control, ablation, appendage occlusion.

Atrial flutterAtrial fibrillation
ActivityOrganised re-entrant circuitChaotic
Atrial rate250 to 350350 to 600
VentriclesOften regularIrregularly irregular
ECGSawtooth F wavesNo P waves
Stroke riskIncreasedHigh
Prevalence2 to 6 million50 to 60 million
The cardiovascular exam begins before the stethoscope: correct vital signs, then careful inspection of the chest, eyes, hands and neck veins, each of which can reveal heart disease.

Heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure, for every patient. Rest 3 to 5 minutes, supine or sitting, no blood draw before; explain; bare arm; never the arm on the mastectomy side or with a problem.

SignMeaning
Vertical sternal scarPrior open-heart surgery
Pectus excavatum or carinatum, hypermobilityPossible Marfan syndrome
XanthelasmaHypercholesterolaemia
Roth spotsInfective endocarditis (about 2 percent)
ClubbingLung disease, chronic hypoxaemia
Osler nodesPainful red lesions; endocarditis
Janeway lesionsPainless red lesions; endocarditis
Splinter haemorrhagesDark nail lines; microemboli

Cyanosis: central is more serious. At Hb 10 g/dL it needs about 70 percent saturation, so cyanosis in severe anaemia means critical illness.

title: Jugular veins and right heart failure
subject: subj:semio

body.html:
Observe the right internal jugular, supine at 15 to 45 degrees, head turned left; press the liver and measure above the sternal angle. Over 4 cm sustained is positive, reflecting right heart function and CVP, not dehydration.

Right heart failure: jugular distension, dependent oedema, ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, anorexia and GI distress; may be cor pulmonale.
Left heart failure means the left ventricle cannot move blood forward well enough, so blood backs up into the lungs. Two types: systolic (can't pump) and diastolic (can't fill).

SystolicDiastolic
ProblemCan't pump hard enoughCan't fill enough
ChambersStretched and thinStiff and thick
Ejection fraction40 percent or lessNormal (about 64 percent)
Stroke volumeLowStill low (poor filling)

SV = EDV minus ESV (135 minus 65 = 70 mL). CO = HR x SV = about 5 L/min. Normal EF 64 to 70 percent; borderline 40 to 50. Frank-Starling: more filling, stronger contraction.

Coronary disease and infarction, valve disease, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis. Hypertension causes hypertrophy, squeezed coronaries and weaker contraction. Diastolic causes: hypertension, aortic stenosis, hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

The kidneys activate renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, retaining fluid to raise preload, which worsens congestion.

Backed-up pulmonary venous pressure makes vessels leak: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, crackles, bloody froth, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (waking 1 to 2 hours after sleep, drowning sensation). Also anxiety, reduced alertness, pallor, sweating, trouble speaking in full sentences. Heart failure also predisposes to arrhythmias.

This revision lecture ties together heart failure and angina, and adds three ideas: the flow equation, endothelial dysfunction as the start of coronary disease, and the global burden of cardiovascular disease.

Q = ΔP / R: raise resistance at the same pressure and flow falls. Left coronary flow happens mainly in diastole.

The endothelium makes nitric oxide, which relaxes smooth muscle. Risk factors cause endothelial dysfunction: less NO, oxidative stress, inflammation, leucocyte adhesion and vasoconstriction (endothelin-1, angiotensin II, thromboxane A2), leading to atherosclerosis, plaque rupture and atherothrombosis.

ConditionKey points
Systolic HFCan't pump, thin chambers
Diastolic HFCan't fill, stiff chambers
Left HFPulmonary oedema, orthopnoea, PND, crackles
Right HFJVD, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, pitting oedema
Stable anginaExertional, relieved by rest, ST depression
Unstable anginaClot on plaque, rest pain, emergency
PrinzmetalSpasm, any time, ST elevation

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide, about 17.7 million a year, though in high-income countries cancer kills twice as many. Over 70 percent is caused by modifiable risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, cholesterol, waist-to-hip ratio, tobacco, alcohol, poor diet, low activity, air pollution, depression. Poor diet, low education, air pollution and low strength matter most in low-income countries, so prevention must be tailored locally.
Right heart failure backs blood up into the body rather than the lungs: swollen neck veins, liver, abdomen and legs. It is most often the consequence of left heart failure.

CauseMechanism
Left heart failureRaised pulmonary pressure overloads the RV (biventricular failure)
Septal defects (ASD, VSD)Left-to-right shunt overloads the right side
Chronic lung diseaseHypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension: cor pulmonale

Chronic hypoxia also causes polycythaemia, inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. Hypoxia symptoms: restlessness, headache, confusion, dyspnoea; severe: tachycardia, tachypnoea, cyanosis.

Jugular venous distension; painful hepatosplenomegaly that may progress to cardiac cirrhosis; ascites; pitting oedema of the legs standing and the sacrum lying down; anorexia, GI distress, weight gain, fatigue.

Pitting gradeDepth
12 mm
23 to 4 mm
35 to 6 mm
48 mm

Left heart failureRight heart failure
Pulmonary congestionPeripheral congestion
Orthopnoea, PND, cracklesJugular distension, oedema
Frothy sputum, cyanosisAscites, hepatomegaly
Activity intoleranceAnorexia, GI distress
The adrenal lecture centres on cortisol excess: recognise the Cushingoid picture, then use ACTH to find the source, and imaging to locate it.

SystemSigns
FatTruncal obesity, moon face
SkinPurple striae, acne
MuscleLimb atrophy
MetabolicDiabetes or prediabetes, hypertension
BoneOsteoporosis
BloodHigh thrombosis risk
MindDepression and suicide risk, or euphoria
SexHirsutism and cycle troubles; erectile dysfunction

ACTHSource
High (ACTH-dependent)Pituitary (Cushing's disease) or ectopic
Low (ACTH-independent)Adrenal

Adrenal CT shows size, lipid structure and extension of an adenoma. MIBG scintigraphy evaluates catecholamine-secreting tissue, including paragangliomas.

Diabetes is chronic hyperglycaemia from an absolute or relative lack of insulin secretion and/or insulin action (insulin resistance). Normal: fasting glucose under 1.10 g/L, and under 1.40 g/L 2 hours after an OGTT.

On the midterm: how diabetes reveals itself (sections 2 to 4).
Three circumstances: by chance (a routine test), from symptoms of hyperglycaemia, or at an acute or chronic complication. Type 2 is diagnosed on average 2 to 3 years after it really starts.

The hyperglycaemia syndrome: polyuria (glycosuria causes an osmotic diuresis), polydipsia (because of the polyuria), weight loss (no insulin, so lipolysis; cells are in a fasting state) and compensatory polyphagia.

  • Also: blurred vision, fatigue (lethargy, even stupor), slow-healing cuts and sores, nausea or abdominal pain, paresthesia (neuropathy), frequent urination at night.
  • Red flags of ketosis (more typical of type 1): acetone breath, Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting.

Examination: capillary blood glucose; urine strip (glucose appears in urine once blood glucose passes 1.8 g/L, the renal threshold); signs of dehydration; weight, height and BMI; signs of infection; look for complications.

1. Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 1.26 g/L (7.0 mmol/L) on 2 samples, or
  2. 2-hour glucose ≥ 2 g/L (11.1 mmol/L) during a 75 g OGTT, or
  3. HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol), or
  4. Classic symptoms with a random glucose ≥ 2 g/L.

Prediabetes: HbA1c 5.7 to 6.4%, fasting 1.00 to 1.25 g/L, 2-hour OGTT 1.40 to 1.99 g/L.

Type 1Type 2
Frequency10 to 15%85 to 90%
AgeYoung (under 40)After 40
OnsetAcuteProgressive
BodyNormal or thinOverweight or obese
Family history++++
Hyperglycaemia symptoms+++Often none
KetosisFrequent, can reveal it (DKA)Absent (DKA only with an added illness)
AutoimmunityAutoantibodies, other autoimmune diseaseNo
Cardiovascular risk factorsNoYes (hypertension, dyslipidaemia...)
InsulinAbsent: insulin for lifeStill made
Complication checkSome years after diagnosisAt diagnosis

• Acute: diabetic ketoacidosis (polyuria, thirst, then abdominal pain, vomiting, fruity breath, dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, drowsiness to coma; ketonaemia ≥ 3 mmol/L, glucose over 2.5 g/L); hypoglycaemia (≤ 0.7 g/L; Whipple triad; adrenergic signs such as tremor, sweating, palpitations, hunger, then neuroglycopenic signs such as confusion, seizures, coma); hyperosmolar state; lactic acidosis.
  • Chronic microvascular: retinopathy (often silent until haemorrhage or detachment: screen with fundoscopy), nephropathy (albumin-to-creatinine ratio, GFR), neuropathy (monofilament, 128 Hz tuning fork, reflexes, DN4; autonomic: orthostatic hypotension, resting tachycardia, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction; Charcot foot, foot ulcers).
  • Chronic macrovascular: coronary disease (often atypical or silent), stroke, peripheral artery disease (lost pulses, cold pale skin, ankle-brachial index).

The pituitary sits in the sella turcica (about 5 × 10 × 15 mm), with the optic chiasm above, the cavernous sinuses on each side and the sphenoid below. Pituitary disease shows itself in three ways: hypersecretion of one axis, insufficiency of one or more axes, and mass effect from the tumour.

On the midterm: prolactinoma, acromegaly and mass effect.

The signs are the same whatever the cause. Prolactin switches off GnRH, so LH and FSH fall: sex-hormone failure plus galactorrhoea (or gynaecomastia).

Clinical features
WomenGalactorrhoea (spontaneous or induced, permanent or intermittent); amenorrhoea (primary or secondary) or oligomenorrhoea; infertility; low libido
MenHypogonadism: low libido is the first symptom; erectile dysfunction; gynaecomastia; infertility
BothMass effect, with macroadenomas only

Tests: prolactin assay with polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation, to exclude macroprolactin; pituitary MRI (micro- or macro/invasive prolactinoma).

PhysiologicalDrugsDisease
Pregnancy, nursing, nipple stimulation, exercise, stress, sleep, seizuresDopamine antagonists (phenothiazines, haloperidol, risperidone, metoclopramide), reserpine, methyldopa, opioids, MAO inhibitors, IV cimetidine, verapamil, TRH testPituitary tumours (prolactinoma, acromegaly, non-secreting adenoma), hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, severe liver failure, stalk lesion (stalk effect), hypophysitis, irradiation, spinal cord lesions, PCOS

• Face: frontal bossing and prominent supraorbital ridges, big nose, prognathism (mandible grows down and forward), teeth separation and malocclusion, coarse features, deep nasolabial furrows, macroglossia and thick lips, deep voice.
  • Extremities and skin: large, thick hands and feet (ring and shoe size go up); thick, oily, sweaty skin.
  • Visceromegaly: thyroid, salivary glands, liver, heart, kidney.
  • Joints and nerves: arthropathy of spine, hips and knees; carpal tunnel syndrome in up to half of patients.
  • Other: sleep apnoea; colonic polyps; hypertension and LV hypertrophy; diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance, hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalciuria, goitre.

Tests: IGF-1; GH during a 75 g OGTT (no suppression = acromegaly); prolactin (often co-secreted); pituitary MRI. Random GH under 0.4 µg/L with a normal IGF-1 rules acromegaly out; GH over 0.4 µg/L during the OGTT confirms it.

• Sideways, into the cavernous sinus: compression of cranial nerves III, IV and VI: diplopia, eyelid ptosis.
  • Upwards, onto the optic chiasm: optic-chiasmatic syndrome: bitemporal visual loss starting in the superior fields (bitemporal superior quadrantanopia, then bitemporal hemianopia); a contralateral homonymous hemianopia can also occur. Rarely: lower acuity, pupil changes, optic atrophy, papilloedema, nystagmus.
  • Pituitary apoplexy: bleeding into a pituitary tumour. A medical emergency: sudden severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, meningism, altered consciousness; often leaves hypopituitarism. Early transsphenoidal decompression (within 8 days).

title: The rest of the lecture (not on this midterm)
subject: subj:semio

body.html:
• Cushing disease: ACTH-dependent cortisol excess, usually an ACTH-secreting microadenoma. Tests: urinary or salivary free cortisol, evening cortisol, 1 mg overnight dexamethasone test, ACTH, pituitary MRI.
  • TSH adenoma (very rare): high FT4 and FT3 with a normal or high TSH.
  • Hypopituitarism: one or more axes fail. Triad: pallor, loss of body hair, depigmentation (areolas, genitals); thin, cold, dry skin. Like Addison's but without dark skin; like hypothyroidism but without goitre.
  • Posterior pituitary: arginine vasopressin deficiency gives polyuria and polydipsia; tell it apart from vasopressin resistance and primary polydipsia.

Thyroid semiology is two opposite syndromes and a lump. Hyperthyroidism speeds everything up; hypothyroidism slows everything down; nodules and goitre need ultrasound and sometimes a needle. TSH and FT4 answer most questions.
The normal thyroid is not visible. Palpate; auscultate for a bruit (high flow, hyperthyroidism). Tests: TSH, FT4, FT3; ultrasound; scintigraphy.

TSH suppressed, FT4/FT3 raised. Weight loss with appetite, resting tachycardia, hot sweaty skin, heat intolerance, fine tremor, hyperreflexia, soft stools, irritability, lid retraction and lid lag.

CauseFeatures
Graves' diseaseCommonest; women 20 to 40; TRAb; diffuse uptake; thyrotoxicosis + goitre + exophthalmos
Toxic adenomaSingle hot nodule, no eye signs
Toxic multinodular goitreOlder patients, multiple hot nodules, compression
ThyroiditisTransient release of stored hormone
Jod-BasedowHyperthyroidism after iodine

TSH raised, FT4/FT3 low. Hypometabolism and asthenia; macrocytic anaemia, hyponatraemia, hypercholesterolaemia, hyperprolactinaemia. Causes: iatrogenic, Hashimoto's and other thyroiditis, iodine deficiency (endemic goitre, cretinism), congenital, central. Complications: myxoedema coma, cardiomyopathy, pericardial effusion, coronary disease.

Goitre: thickness over 2.5 cm, volume over 18 cm³ (women) or 20 cm³ (men). 90 to 95 percent of lumps are benign. Red flags: hoarseness, nodes, stridor. Ultrasound grades U1 to U5; FNAC for U3 to U5. Up to 50 percent of people have microscopic nodules.

GI bleeding is blood loss through the digestive tract, visible or occult; a medical and surgical emergency. Management: assess severity, stabilise and resuscitate, find the cause, give specific (often endoscopic) treatment. The approach has three levels: positive (is it digestive?), topographic (upper or lower?), etiological (which lesion?).

Haematemesis: vomiting of red or black blood, sometimes with food or clots, often after nausea; a lesion above the angle of Treitz. Differentials: haemoptysis (frothy, after coughing), swallowed epistaxis, gum bleeding, coloured food or drugs. Melaena: black, tarry, foul-smelling stools of digested blood; usually upper GI, but possibly small bowel or right colon; appears 6 to 8 hours after bleeding starts; differentials: iron, charcoal, bismuth, some foods. Haematochezia: bright red blood per anus, sometimes clots; suggests colon, rectum or anus, or a massive upper bleed with rapid transit. Occult bleeding: chronic minimal loss shown by a faecal occult blood test or microcytic anaemia; a massive non-externalised bleed can present as shock without visible blood (gastric aspiration or rectal exam).

Warning signs: pallor, cold extremities, restlessness, tachycardia; severe: hypotension, polypnoea, oliguria, altered consciousness, mottling. Haemoglobin and haematocrit fall, but a normal haemoglobin does not exclude recent bleeding. Haematemesis with melaena or rectal bleeding means abundant bleeding.

Emergency: emergency or intensive care unit; two large-bore IV lines; CBC, blood group and cross-match, ionogram, creatinine, liver tests; crystalloids and transfusion as needed; oxygen; gastric tube and urinary catheter; continuous monitoring of blood pressure, pulse, urine output and consciousness.

History: peptic ulcer, liver disease, anticoagulants, NSAIDs, aspirin; sudden or progressive onset, pain; asthenia, weight loss, diarrhoea. Examination: epigastric tenderness (ulcer, gastritis), signs of liver disease or portal hypertension (varices), rectal examination (melaena, haematochezia, haemorrhoids, fissure, mass). Upper GI endoscopy: first line in any suspected upper bleed, urgent after stabilisation; diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic; finds the source in over 90%. Lower: anoscopy and rectoscopy, colonoscopy (key test); enteroscopy or capsule if no source.

Upper causes: peptic ulcer, oesophageal or gastric varices (portal hypertension), Mallory-Weiss tear (after vomiting), erosive gastritis or duodenitis, cancer, stress ulcers, NSAID or aspirin lesions. Lower causes: anal (haemorrhoids, fissure, fistula, cancer); colorectal (cancer, polyps, diverticular disease, angiodysplasia, IBD); small bowel (vascular malformations, tumours, Meckel's diverticulum in the young).

Supportive: volume resuscitation, oxygen, transfusion, proton pump inhibitors for a suspected peptic cause. Endoscopic haemostasis: injection (adrenaline, sclerosant), thermal coagulation, haemoclips, variceal band ligation; surgery for refractory bleeding or perforation. Prognosis depends on the cause (variceal and malignant worse), initial severity, comorbidities and speed of management. Causes vary with age: ulcers and varices in adults, polyps or cancer in the elderly, Meckel's in the young.

Constipation is easy to diagnose; the work is finding the cause. First rule out a secondary (organic) cause, especially when there are red flags; then type a primary constipation as slow transit or outlet dysfunction.

Fewer than 3 stools a week, under 100 g/day, hard stools.

TypeMechanismCauses
Slow transitReduced colonic motilityColonic inertia, spastic colon
Outlet dysfunctionPelvic floor fails to relaxAnismus, megarectum, rectocele, internal prolapse
SecondaryUnderlying diseaseTumour, hypothyroidism, diabetes, Parkinson's, opioids, iron

History of drugs, diet, surgery, family cancer. Exam: absent bowel sounds (ileus) versus hyperactive (obstruction). Digital rectal exam: impaction, tone, masses, pelvic floor.

Red flags: rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, severe pain, family history of colorectal cancer or IBD.

Organic: colonoscopy, CT or MRI, blood count, thyroid, calcium and potassium, glucose, coeliac serology. Functional: colonic transit, defecography, anorectal manometry for outlet dysfunction. IBS-C: pain and bloating without organic disease.

Diarrhoea is the passage of loose or watery stools with more frequency and/or volume: over 300 g/day, more than 3 per day, over 90% water. By duration: acute (under 2 weeks: infection, food poisoning), prolonged (2 to 4 weeks: post-infectious, parasitic), chronic (over 4 weeks: IBD, coeliac disease, pancreatic insufficiency). Reason in steps: duration, stool aspect, associated signs, mechanism.

Differential diagnoses: false diarrhoea (small hard stools, under 300 g/day), anal incontinence, non-faecal discharge (blood, pus, mucus without stool).

Very frequent, usually benign and self-limiting, but dangerous in infants, the elderly and the immunocompromised, and sometimes reveals a chronic disease. Two mechanisms: secretory (choleriform): an enterotoxin drives massive water and salt secretion (cholera, enterotoxigenic E. coli), profuse watery stools, dehydration, persists during fasting; invasive (dysenteric): mucosal invasion (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter), bloody mucous stools, fever, pain, tenesmus.

Severity: context (extreme ages, immunosuppression, cardiac, renal or liver disease), dehydration (dry tongue, thirst, skin fold, hypotension, oliguria), complications (dysenteric colitis, sepsis). Orientation: recent meals, collective cases, tropical travel, antibiotics (C. difficile), HIV or chemotherapy; stool frequency, volume, blood or pus; vomiting, pain, tenesmus. Tests only if: severe dehydration, blood or pus, fever over 38 °C, duration over 3 days, epidemic context or immunosuppression: CBC, CRP, electrolytes, renal function; stool culture and parasitology; CT or colonoscopy if complicated.

Over 4 weeks, from malabsorption, secretion, osmotic effect, accelerated transit or exudative protein loss. History: onset, frequency, relation to meals and time of day, stool aspect (liquid, greasy, bloody, mucous), weight loss, fever, pain, drugs (NSAIDs, laxatives, antibiotics), family history (IBD, cancer, coeliac). Examination: hydration and nutrition, abdomen, mandatory digital rectal exam, extra-abdominal signs (nodes, skin, joints, eyes, thyroid).

Tests: first line CBC, CRP, electrolytes, liver tests, protein electrophoresis, calcium, vitamin D, ferritin, albumin (severity, malabsorption); second line TSH, HIV serology, anti-transglutaminase antibodies, stool parasitology; endoscopy: gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies, colonoscopy with ileal and colonic biopsies (IBD, coeliac, microscopic colitis); imaging: ultrasound, CT enterography, MRI.

Malabsorptive: abundant, greasy, pale, foul-smelling stools; weight loss, anaemia, bone pain, brittle nails; small-bowel disease (coeliac, Crohn's, Whipple, lymphoma, giardiasis), pancreatic insufficiency, bile-salt deficiency. Motor: accelerated transit; post-prandial, urgent, improves with fasting; hyperthyroidism, diabetes, carcinoid tumour, gastrectomy, IBS. Osmotic: osmotically active substances (mannitol, lactulose, laxatives, lactase deficiency); stops with fasting; no blood, no general deterioration. Secretory: active hypersecretion; persists during fasting; IBD, endocrine tumours (VIPoma), microscopic colitis, infections, drugs (colchicine, digitalis). Exudative: plasma protein loss into the gut, diagnosed by alpha-1 antitrypsin clearance; lymphangiectasia, lymphoma, cirrhosis, ulcerative colitis.

Dysentery is the rectum sounding an alarm: pain, false urges and stools made of mucus, pus and blood. The causes range from infection to IBD to cancer, so the key tools are the rectal exam, sigmoidoscopy and stool tests.
Cramps focused on the left iliac fossa with urgency; tenesmus, a painful urge with an empty rectum; false urges; non-faecal stools of mucus, pus and blood; fever, weight loss, dehydration.

Look for dehydration, fever, tachycardia, hypotension (severe dehydration or sepsis), tenderness, and rectal lesions, blood or mucus.

TestPurpose
Blood count, CRP, electrolytesSystematic
C. difficile toxinAfter recent antibiotics
Stool microscopyRBC, WBC, Entamoeba histolytica
Stool cultureShigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli
Sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopyConfirm, biopsy
CTComplications, severe or atypical cases
Colorectal cancer and polyps, IBD, infectious proctitis (Entamoeba, CMV, E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella), radiation colitis, ischaemic colitis.

Dysphagia is difficulty or discomfort swallowing solids or liquids from mouth to stomach. It is always an alarm sign: any adult with progressive dysphagia has oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise, and upper GI endoscopy is the key test. Distinguish it from odynophagia (painful swallowing), aphagia (complete inability) and globus (lump sensation without real difficulty); always clarify what the patient means.

Swallowing has three phases: oral (voluntary), pharyngeal (reflex laryngeal closure and propulsion), oesophageal (involuntary peristalsis). By level: oropharyngeal (high): difficulty starting, cough, nasal regurgitation; neurological, muscular or ENT causes; oesophageal (low): food sticking behind the sternum. By mechanism: organic/mechanical (tumour, peptic stricture, foreign body) vs functional/motor (achalasia, diffuse spasm, scleroderma).

Age: in the elderly always rule out cancer. Risk factors: alcohol, tobacco, caustics, GERD, radiotherapy, surgery. Onset: sudden (foreign body, spasm), progressive (cancer, peptic stricture), intermittent (motor). Food type: solids then liquids → organic; liquids as much as or more than solids → motor (paradoxical dysphagia, achalasia). Associated signs: odynophagia (infection, inflammation), heartburn and regurgitation (reflux, stricture), cough at meals and nasal regurgitation (oropharyngeal), hoarseness (larynx), weight loss and asthenia (cancer); night cough or hiccups (reflux, compression).

Examination: general state (weight loss, malnutrition, dehydration), neck (lymph nodes suggest cancer, thyroid masses), ENT (mouth, oropharynx, larynx), neurology (cranial nerves IX, X, XI, XII, stroke, neuromuscular disease). Intermittent → functional; constant and progressive → organic.

Tests: upper GI endoscopy first line (mucosa, biopsies, obstruction); barium swallow (motility, Zenker's diverticulum); oesophageal manometry (peristalsis, LES relaxation); CT or endoscopic ultrasound (staging, extrinsic compression); laryngoscopy (ENT).

Oesophageal causes: cancer of the oesophagus or cardia (recent, progressive solids → liquids, weight loss, smoking and alcohol; endoscopy with biopsy confirms); peptic stricture (long reflux history, slow, mainly solids, no early deterioration); achalasia (solids and liquids from the start, paradoxical, intermittent, worse with hot or cold foods, general state preserved; manometry shows absent peristalsis and a non-relaxing LES); foreign body, benign tumours, caustic stenosis, infectious oesophagitis (Candida, HSV, TB). Extra-oesophageal: compression (mediastinal tumours, thoracic aortic aneurysm, large left atrium); ENT (tonsillitis, pharyngitis, oral candidiasis; pharyngeal, laryngeal and thyroid cancers; Zenker's diverticulum); neurological and muscular (stroke, Parkinson's, ALS, MS, myasthenia, myopathies).

Refer urgently: age over 50, rapidly progressive dysphagia, weight loss over 5 kg, iron-deficiency anaemia, history of caustics, GERD or radiation. Complications: aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition and dehydration, complete obstruction (aphagia), cancer progression or perforation.
The digestive exam goes from mouth to neck to abdomen to anus, with the abdomen examined in four steps: inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation.

Check identity, explain, consent, private warm room; patient flat, doctor on the right.

Oral signMeaning
Aphthous ulcersE.g. inflammatory bowel disease
Atrophic glossitisVitamin B12 deficiency
White tongue plaquesCandidiasis
Angular cheilitisIron deficiency anaemia

Neck: the left supraclavicular node signals digestive cancer metastasis; thyroid moves on swallowing.

Nine regions. Inspection: scars, hernia, eventration, collateral veins (portal hypertension), bulges. Palpation: knees bent, light then deep; liver under the right ribs with a deep breath; the normal spleen is hard to feel. Percussion: tympanic except the liver and a full bladder. Auscultation: bowel sounds and arterial bruits.
Consent, privacy, knee-chest or Sims position, gloves and lubricant; inspect, then digitally examine the anal canal, distal rectum and prostate.

GERD is reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus causing symptoms and/or complications. It is one of the commonest digestive complaints, chronic and relapsing, and severity depends on lesions and complications. Physiological reflux is transient, post-prandial, asymptomatic and harmless; pathological reflux is frequent or prolonged and causes symptoms, inflammation or complications.

At rest the lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) and the diaphragmatic crura prevent reflux; weakness or transient relaxation lets contents rise. Factors: LES hypotonia, hiatal hernia (the commonest anatomical cause), raised intra-abdominal pressure (obesity, pregnancy, tight clothing), delayed gastric emptying. Foods lowering LES tone: fats, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, mint, spicy food. Drugs: nitrates, theophylline, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers, progesterone, sedatives. Lifestyle: smoking, alcohol, large or late meals.

Pyrosis (heartburn), the most characteristic: retrosternal burning rising from the epigastrium to the throat, post-prandial or nocturnal, triggered by bending forward, lying down or heavy meals, worsened by fatty or acidic food, chocolate, coffee, alcohol, mint, relieved by antacids. Regurgitation: effortless return of acid contents into the mouth, hot bitter taste. Others: epigastric burning, belching, bloating, nausea, early satiety, water brash.

Extra-digestive: ENT and oral (dental erosions, gingivitis, chronic pharyngitis and laryngitis, globus, hoarseness); respiratory (chronic nocturnal cough, asthma-like symptoms from micro-aspiration, bronchitis, laryngospasm); non-cardiac chest pain mimicking angina. These atypical forms can delay diagnosis.

Typical forms (heartburn + regurgitation): the diagnosis is clinical. Tests are reserved for atypical or extra-digestive forms, alarm signs, poor response to treatment, age over 50 or long-standing reflux. Alarm signs: dysphagia, odynophagia, GI bleeding (haematemesis, melaena), iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss, vomiting or obstruction; all require endoscopy.

Upper GI endoscopy (alarm signs, atypical symptoms, age over 50, treatment failure) shows peptic oesophagitis, stricture or Barrett's oesophagus; a normal endoscopy does not exclude GERD (non-erosive reflux disease, NERD). 24-hour pH-metry is the reference test: GERD confirmed if pH < 4 for more than 5% of the time; useful in atypical forms and NERD. Manometry (LES pressure, motility), impedance (non-acid reflux), barium swallow (stricture, hernia).

Peptic oesophagitis; bleeding (haematemesis, anaemia); peptic stricture with dysphagia; Barrett's oesophagus (metaplasia with cancer risk); respiratory complications (chronic cough, asthma, aspiration).
Hepatomegaly is diagnosed by the examining hand. How the liver feels (soft or hard, smooth or nodular, painful or not) points to the cause; ultrasound confirms.

Palpate the lower border with deep inspiration and hooked fingers; percuss the upper limit from above; measure on the midclavicular line: normal under 12 cm. Normal liver: firm, regular, smooth, painless.

Differential: left: stomach, transverse colon, pancreas; right: liver ptosis, Riedel lobe, colon, right kidney, gallbladder.

Jaundice is excess bilirubin (above about 35 µmol/L). The key first question: is it cholestatic (conjugated) or not (unconjugated)? Everything else follows.

Bilirubin comes from haemoglobin breakdown and leaves in bile. Diagnosis of jaundice is clinical.

Cholestasis: pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, steatorrhoea, xanthoma and xanthelasma, ADEK deficiency. Labs: conjugated bilirubin, GGT, ALP, cholesterol up; prothrombin time prolonged.

Hepatitis risks, alcohol, drugs, travel, surgery, family history. Acute cholangitis = pain, fever, jaundice. Examine consciousness, asterixis, fetor hepaticus, skin (scratch marks, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia), abdomen, rectum and nodes.

Ultrasound comes first; ERCP is therapeutic.

Nausea and vomiting are among the most common GI complaints, with many causes, from minor digestive disease to serious neurological or systemic illness. The work is to describe the vomiting well, look for alarm symptoms and complications, then find the cause, digestive or not.

Nausea: an unpleasant, subjective sensation, often with the urge to vomit, from the GI tract or the CNS. Vomiting (emesis): the forceful expulsion of stomach contents through the mouth, usually preceded by nausea; an active mechanism of violent cyclic contractions of the abdominal muscles, diaphragm and respiratory muscles.

Triggers: GI irritation, vestibular disturbances, higher cortical centres, and the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) stimulated by drugs or toxins. They activate the vomiting centre, then the abdominal vagal afferents; the diaphragm and abdominal muscles contract strongly while the LES relaxes, and stomach contents are forcefully ejected.

History: age, medical and surgical (especially digestive) history, medications (type, dose, date of last intake), toxic exposure, recent travel, similar cases in contacts, last menstrual period and contraception.

Characteristics: onset and duration (acute under 2 weeks, chronic over 3 weeks on the summary slide; or recurrent), spontaneous or induced, frequency, content, volume, triggers (diet, head position), impact (appetite, hydration, weight).

Associated symptoms: nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, myalgias, fever; extra-digestive: headache, photophobia (meningeal syndrome), altered consciousness.

General: dehydration (dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes), vital signs, temperature. Abdomen: distension, scars, tenderness, masses; hyperactive bowel sounds suggest obstruction, absent sounds ileus; percussion for ascites or a mass. Neurological: headache and papilledema (raised ICP); altered mental status, dizziness, nystagmus (CNS cause). Cardiovascular: heart failure. Lymph nodes: infection or malignancy.

Alarm symptoms: persistent vomiting or inability to keep oral intake, severe or progressive pain, haematemesis, fever, neurological symptoms, dehydration, weight loss, bilious or feculent vomiting (obstruction), elderly patient, immunocompromised state.

Aims: initial work-up of the cause, detect complications, guide decisions; the choice depends on the presentation.

Labs: CBC, electrolytes (Na, K, Cl, HCO3), renal function, glucose (DKA), hCG in women of reproductive age, thyroid tests if hyperthyroidism is suspected, urinalysis (ketones).

Upper GI endoscopy (allows biopsy): suspected mucosal lesion, obstruction, complications (bleeding, oesophagitis, gastritis); finds ulcers, erosions, masses, chronic GERD or Barrett's. Ultrasound: gallbladder, liver, pancreas, kidneys. CT: obstruction, pancreatitis. ECG (hypokalaemia), cerebral CT, endocrine or toxicological tests if indicated.

Differential diagnosis: gastro-oesophageal regurgitation and rumination syndrome, both without nausea.

The chest exam runs in four steps, always comparing left with right: inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation. The goal is to group the signs into a syndrome, such as consolidation, effusion or pneumothorax.

Bare chest, seated or standing, in full light; watch the patient undress. Note general appearance and the thorax shape.

Work of breathing: accessory muscles, nasal flaring, retractions, grunting, pursed lips, paradoxical breathing. Pierre Marie osteoarthropathy: painful clubbing with periostitis, hereditary or paraneoplastic.

Tactile fremitus (toy boat, 44, 33): increased in pneumonia; decreased or abolished in pleurisy, pneumothorax, atelectasis and emphysema bullae.

Percussion compares both sides level by level. Normal lung resonant; liver and heart dull. Dullness: pleurisy, pachypleuritis, consolidation. Hyperresonance: pneumothorax, emphysema.

Normal sounds: vesicular (both lungs, inspiration and early expiration), bronchial (sternum), tracheal (neck).

The general exam adds heart (right heart failure, pericarditis), abdomen (ascites, organomegaly), ENT, lymph nodes, urogenital and neurological findings; in pleurisy, report pericarditis, ascites and meningeal signs.

Five symptoms carry respiratory medicine: cough, sputum, vomica, hemoptysis, chest pain and dyspnoea. For each, the exam asks the same things: define it, analyse it (onset, duration, timing, triggers, appearance) and list the causes.

A deep inspiration with an open glottis, then an explosive expiration: a defence reflex to clear the airways. Productive cough should be respected; useless dry cough treated.

Chronic bronchitis: productive morning cough at least 3 months a year for 2 consecutive years. Dry chronic cough: cancer, interstitial disease, asthma, rhinosinusitis, GERD, ACE inhibitors, psychogenic. Complications: syncope, pneumothorax, rib fracture, incontinence, hernia, vomiting, insomnia.

Sputum is abnormal subglottic secretion; over 30 mL/day is excessive, over 100 mL/day bronchorrhoea. The mucociliary escalator is impaired in smokers, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis and ciliary dyskinesia.

Fluid between the pleural layers: progressive pain, dry cough, dyspnoea, often fever. A large effusion pushes the trachea away.

Thoracentesis is done sitting, in the zone of dullness, above the lower rib; it confirms the effusion, shows its appearance and gives samples. Exudate: albumin over 30 g/L (inflammatory). Transudate: under 30 g/L (mechanical). Biopsy or thoracoscopy find the cause.

Air in the pleura, spontaneous, traumatic or iatrogenic; primary (no lesion) or secondary. Air enters through a visceral breach (ruptured bleb) or a parietal one (wound). Sudden stabbing pain, dyspnoea, dry cough; distended hemithorax, hyperresonance, absent breath sounds. Imaging shows lucency without markings, the visceral pleural line, and mediastinal shift away. Treated by needle aspiration.

Mixed: opacity topped by lucency. Hydro-, pyo-, haemo- or chylopneumothorax by the fluid.

Consolidation: a lobe no longer ventilates; increased fremitus, dullness, bronchial breathing, crackles; alveolar opacity with air bronchogram. Non-retracted: pneumonia, infarction, tuberculous pneumonia. Retracted: bronchial obstruction or destruction, structures pulled toward it.

Emphysema: centrilobular (blue bloater) or panlobular (pink puffer); barrel chest, diffuse hyperresonance.

Cavity: tuberculosis, abscess, excavated cancer, hydatid cyst.
